bio.en: Kristen Berman is the CEO and co-founder of Irrational Labs, a behavioral-design firm that helps companies like Google, Airbnb, and Microsoft build better products, and co-founded the Common Cents Lab at Duke.
bio.zh: 克里斯滕·伯曼（Kristen Berman）是行为设计公司 Irrational Labs 的 CEO 兼联合创始人，该公司帮助 Google、Airbnb、微软等企业打造更好的产品；她还联合创办了杜克大学的 Common Cents Lab。

summary.en: Kristen explains how behavioral science reveals that people act on emotion and social norms, not pure rationality, and how products can be designed to steer better behavior. She introduces the 3B Framework of Behavioral Design with real case studies, including work with TikTok. The episode shows how to apply psychology to drive engagement and growth without manipulation.
summary.zh: 克里斯滕解释了行为科学如何揭示：人是基于情绪与社会规范行事，而非纯粹理性，以及产品如何被设计来引导更好的行为。她以 TikTok 等真实案例介绍了"行为设计 3B 框架"。本期展示了如何运用心理学推动用户参与和增长，且不带操纵色彩。

turns.speaker: Kristen Berman
turns.en: Economics says, "Look, people are rational. We make decisions with no emotion. We use lots of computational energy, weigh the pros and cons." I mean, obviously, that's just not true. It ignores the whole field of psychology. And so, in behavioral economics, you combine the field of psychology and economics and say, "Look, people make decisions with lots of emotion. We are present bias. We over-weighed our present selves. We follow social norms." But the good news is that we do these things in predictable ways. And once you understand how and why people behave, you can start to change it. And so, behavioral science and behavioral design basically uses those insights on psychology to actually apply it within real world problems.
turns.zh: 经济学家会说：“看，人是理性的。我们做决策时不受情绪影响，充分权衡利弊。”但显然这根本不正确——它忽视了整个心理学领域。因此，在行为经济学中，我们将心理学与经济学相结合，指出：“看，人们做决策时充满情绪。我们受制于现状偏差，过度重视当下自我，还会追随社会规范。”不过好消息是，人们的这些行为模式是可预测的。一旦你理解了人们行为背后的机制和原因，就能着手改变现状。因此，行为科学和行为设计实质上是将心理学研究成果应用于现实世界问题的解决中。

turns.zh: 完全正确。看到我们的客户如Square、Spotify和Zuora能够在Flatfile平台上成功发展业务，这一点确实令人信服。这是因为[此处语音不清，00:02:50]数据导入机制就像一剂催化剂，助力他们和他们的客户更快地达成业务目标。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Kristen, welcome to the podcast.
turns.zh: 克里斯汀，欢迎做客我们的播客节目。

turns.speaker: Kristen Berman
turns.en: Thanks, Lenny. Great to be here.
turns.zh: 谢谢你，莱尼。很高兴能来这里。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's great to have you. You're on something called Irrational Labs, and so, to set a little context for folks, can you just talk about what it is you all do at Irrational Labs?
turns.zh: 很高兴您能加入我们。你们所在的公司叫做Irrational Labs，所以为了让大家更好地了解情况，能否先讲讲Irrational Labs团队的主要业务方向？

turns.speaker: Kristen Berman
turns.en: Yeah, so Irrational Labs, we are a behavioral science consulting and design shop. So, we think about all things behavior change. We work on understanding psychologies that drive users, and then designing and testing ways to change behavior and drive engagement.
turns.zh: 是的，Irrational Labs是一家行为科学咨询与设计公司。我们致力于研究一切与行为改变相关的课题。我们专注于理解影响用户行为的心理机制，并通过设计和测试各类方法来改变用户行为、提升用户参与度。

turns.speaker: Kristen Berman
turns.en: I started it in 2013 with Dan Ariely, who's a famed behavioral economist. We started just working with a handful of companies, and now we have a team of 20 behavioral scientists working on behavior change across industries.
turns.zh: 2013年，我与著名的行为经济学家丹·阿里利（Dan Ariely）共同创立了这个项目。最初我们只与少数几家公司合作，如今已拥有一支由20名行为科学家组成的团队，致力于推动各行业的行为改变。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Can you talk about some of the companies that you've worked with, just to give us some examples? And then, what kind of stuff have you actually helped them with?
turns.zh: 您能否谈谈您曾合作过的部分公司，举几个例子供我们参考？然后，您具体为这些公司提供了哪些方面的帮助？

turns.speaker: Kristen Berman
turns.en: We started a lot of our work at Google. We were actually embedded within Google for around three years. I even had a bus pass. And we started their behavioral economics team. We worked with over 25 teams from like self-driving cars to YouTube. And so, that was a big piece of the early work. And then recently, we've done work with TikTok where we've tried to... It actually accomplished decreasing misinformation share by 24%. We worked with one medical on how to increase setting doctor's appointments right away during the onboarding, and that worked and drove it up by 20%. We worked with Credit Karma on basically helping them increase set up for reoccurring deposits. We did that and increased it by 18%. So, basically a variety of ways to drive behavior change. Done stuff with Intuit, Microsoft, LinkedIn, and obviously, a variety of startups as well.
turns.zh: 我们在谷歌开展了许多工作。实际上，我们在谷歌内部工作了约三年时间。我甚至还持有谷歌的公交卡通行证。我们还组建了谷歌的行为经济学团队，与超过25个团队展开合作，涵盖从自动驾驶汽车到YouTube等多个领域。这是早期工作的核心部分。近年来，我们与TikTok合作，成功将虚假信息传播率降低了24%。我们与一家医疗机构合作，帮助他们提升新用户注册时的即时预约率，最终成功提升了20%。我们还与Credit Karma合作，帮助他们提高重复存款的设置成功率，最终将该项数据提升了18%。总之，我们通过多种方式推动行为改变。此外，我们还与Intuit、微软、领英等公司，以及众多初创企业开展了合作。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow. Okay, we're definitely going to talk about some of those examples. I'm super curious to hear what you did with TikTok, big company and story these days. Before we get to that, what exactly is behavioral design, and can you just define this space for us?
turns.zh: 哇哦。好的，我们肯定会探讨其中的一些案例。我特别好奇想听听你最近在TikTok上的尝试、以及关于大公司和成功案例的分享。在深入这些话题之前，您能先为我们定义一下"行为设计"这个概念吗？

turns.speaker: Kristen Berman
turns.en: Let's start with what is behavioral economics? So, basically, behavioral economics is a reaction to economics. So, economics says, "Look, people are rational. We make decisions with no emotion. We use lots of computational energy, weigh the pros and cons." I mean, obviously, that's just not true. It ignores the whole field of psychology. And so, in behavioral economics, you combine the field of psychology and economics and say, "Look, people make decisions with lots of emotion. We are present bias. We over-weighed our present selves. We follow social norms." But the good news is that we do these things in predictable ways. And once you understand how and why people behave, you can start to change it. And so, behavioral science and behavioral design basically uses those insights on psychology to actually apply it within real world problems.
turns.zh: 先来解释一下什么是行为经济学。简单来说，行为经济学是对传统经济学的反思。传统经济学认为："人是理性的，做决策时不受情绪影响，充分计算利弊"。但显然这种假设并不成立——它忽视了心理学领域的研究成果。因此，行为经济学将心理学与经济学相结合，指出："人类的决策充满情绪波动，我们受制于现状偏见、高估当下自我、追随社会规范"。但好消息是，这些行为模式具有可预测性。一旦理解了人们行为背后的心理机制，我们就能有针对性地加以改变。因此，行为科学和行为设计正是利用这些心理学洞见，将其应用于现实世界的决策优化中。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What are some of the biggest surprises, or maybe unintuitive results that you've come across working with companies using these insights in behavioral design, behavioral economics?
turns.zh: 在与那些将行为设计和行为经济学见解应用于实践的公司合作过程中，你们遇到过哪些最令人惊讶，或者说最出乎意料的结果呢？

turns.speaker: Kristen Berman
turns.en: Yeah, great question. One story that recently happened is actually a surprise that happened to the client. The partner was shocked. It actually didn't surprise us. And so, this was with a popular FinTech app and their most requested feature was budgeting. So, it came through all the support forums, interviews, felt like a table stakes feature; people wanted budgeting. And so, if you're the PM there, you're probably like, "You may talk to a few other users. You may get some confirmation, but you're likely building budgeting." And that's really where they were when we came and started working with them. We couldn't move them in another direction, but we did convince them to do an experiment. So, we convinced them to test, and there was three conditions. One was the control, which is just telling people how much they spend, and the other two were variations on budgeting. So, two different ways to do budgeting.
turns.zh: 是的，问得好！最近遇到的一个案例，着实让客户大吃一惊，合作伙伴也感到震惊。但其实这对我们来说并不意外。当时是一款热门金融科技应用，其最受期待的功能是预算管理。通过各种支持论坛和用户访谈，我们发现用户普遍认为这是一项基本功能——大家都渴望能进行预算管理。作为项目经理，面对这种共识，你大概会想：“再去征求几位用户意见，确认一下需求，但最终肯定还是要开发预算功能。”这正是我们介入合作前，他们的项目进展阶段。我们无法改变他们的方向，但成功说服他们开展了一项实验。实验设定了三个条件：一个是控制组，仅告知用户消费金额；另外两个组则分别测试两种预算管理方案。

turns.speaker: Kristen Berman
turns.en: So, big experiment. This is with 10,000 people, so we can really trust the results. And what happened? Nothing. So, they were shocked. The team was shocked. Remember, this is a big investment of time and effort, took a lot of energy to build. Zero change in average spend, zero change in spend variability. And so, the question is: Why weren't we surprised? Why were they surprised? The thinking here is if you map out every single step that it takes to do this behavior, and the behavior would be reducing your spend, it's pretty clear that budgeting just isn't going to pull the weight. And this is what we call a behavioral diagnosis, where you map out every single step. So, you'd have to know what your budget is. You'd have to know where in the month you are. You'd have to make a plan to do it. You then have to do it multiple times during the month. Incredibly difficult to do this one behavior. And once you do that behavioral diagnosis and you map out... We try to understand what people actually do versus what they say they will do. And by doing that, it becomes wildly clear that we should all be skeptical that budgeting would actually work to change the behavior that you're trying to get to.
turns.zh: 好的，这是一项大型实验，涉及1万名参与者，因此我们可以充分信赖实验结果。但结果如何呢？毫无变化。整个团队都大吃一惊。要知道，这项研究耗费了大量时间和精力，花费了巨大心血。平均消费额毫无变化，消费波动性也丝毫未减。那么问题来了：为什么我们不感到惊讶？为什么他们会如此震惊？关键在于，如果你完整地剖析实现这一行为所需的每一步——而减少消费就是一个典型行为——就会发现预算工具根本无法发挥作用。这种分析过程被称为行为诊断，即系统性地拆解每个行为步骤。首先，你得清楚自己的预算额，掌握当前月份的进度，然后制定具体计划，最后在月内多次践行。但这种行为习惯的养成实在太难了。通过行为诊断，我们能清晰发现：人们实际行为与口头承诺之间存在巨大落差。由此可见，我们对预算能有效改变行为的信心必须打上折扣。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, I'm also not surprised that didn't have a big impact. I have so many apps with budgeting features and I've tried many times to use them and it never sticks. It's like, "Eh, I'm just going to..." It's too much work.
turns.zh: 是啊，我也不奇怪它没能产生太大影响。我下载过很多带有预算功能的应用，也尝试过多次使用它们，但始终无法坚持下去。总觉得：“哎呀，我还是算了吧……” 毕竟这实在太费功夫了。

turns.speaker: Kristen Berman
turns.en: It's way too much work. And so, sometimes, any kind of work that we put on the user, we should be skeptical. We have to really prove that it's worth their time, and then measure if they actually do it.
turns.zh: 这工作量实在太大了。所以，有时候，我们给用户布置任何任务时，都应该保持怀疑态度。我们必须切实证明这项任务值得他们花费时间，然后再去衡量他们是否真的会去执行。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Is there a better approach to that specific problem that you've found, or is that too broad of a question?
turns.zh: 针对那个特定问题，你是否找到了更好的解决方法？或者说这个问题问得是否太宽泛了？

turns.speaker: Kristen Berman
turns.en: The first line of defense in any problem solving would be, how would you make it easier for somebody to do? And so, in the personal finance world, really, the answer to most things is just default. So, it worked for automatic enrollment 401(k). The reason we have retirement savings in America is because people are defaulted into saving from their paycheck. So, that would be first line of defense. Obviously, difficult for product teams to execute on, takes a lot of backend infrastructure. So, if we were just solving the personal financial management stuff of like a budgeting alternative, we'd actually go to making it not just logistically easier, but cognitively easier. So, we call them rules of thumb; instead of having to decide in the moment, do I do this thing? And you're weighing the pros and cons. It's kind of typical econ, like, how much is this $3 worth to me? You'd actually make a rule of thumb that says, "Do I do it, or not?" So, instead of deciding, do you take a Lyft when you're coming home from work, you'd have a rule of thumb that says, "I don't take Lyft on the weekdays. I take it on the weekends." Very simple now to actually make this kind of decision. It's a heuristic . It's not going to be perfect, but it's going to help you reduce your spend in an easier way, at least, in a way that you'd stayed adherent to.
turns.zh:
解决任何问题时的首要防线都是：如何让用户更容易完成任务？在个人理财领域，大多数问题的答案其实都是默认选项。比如自动加入401(k)计划的功能之所以能成功，就是因为美国的退休储蓄体系通过从用户工资中自动扣除的方式实现了默认储蓄。这就是第一道防线。但显然，产品团队要实现这样的功能难度很大，需要强大的后台基础设施支持。

如果我们只想解决预算管理等个人理财难题，关键在于让用户的决策过程不仅更符合逻辑，更符合认知习惯。我们称之为"经验法则"。用户无需在当下权衡利弊，而是可以根据既定规则快速行动。例如，用户可能纠结于"下班回家时该不该叫Lyft车"，但通过制定规则"工作日不叫Lyft，周末可以"，就能轻松做出选择。这是一种启发式决策，虽然不完美，但至少能帮助用户更轻松地控制开支，且更容易坚持下去。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It reminds me a bit of James Clears' idea of creating this identity for yourself where he is like, "If you're like, 'I am a person that doesn't take Lyft on the weekdays', that becomes kind of this identity component and that makes it easier for you not to do that." Is that related?
turns.zh: 这让我想起了詹姆斯·克利尔（James Clear）提出的为自己塑造身份的理念。他举例说：“如果你对自己说：‘我是一个平日不乘坐Lyft的人’，那么这就形成了一个身份标签，让你更容易坚持不乘坐Lyft。” 这两者有联系吗？

turns.speaker: Kristen Berman
turns.en: Yeah, basically. Sometimes, we think behavior change is driven by our attitudes, our preferences like, "I really want to be a runner" or "I really like this thing." But in reality, our behavior is driven by what we do. So, in order to change behavior, you have to do something different. It's not enough to have a goal objective to do it. And I think, maybe that's the big annoying thing about the self-help industry. It kind of just tells you it's enough to have a goal. It's not enough. You actually need to redesign your environment to change your behavior.
turns.zh: 是啊，大体来说确实如此。有时候，我们以为行为改变是由态度或个人偏好驱动的，比如“我真的想成为一名跑步者”或者“我特别喜欢这件东西”。但实际上，我们的行为是由行动本身所驱动的。因此，要想改变行为，就必须采取不同的行动。仅有目标是远远不够的。我觉得，这或许正是自助行业最令人厌烦的地方——它总告诉你只要设定目标就行，但这远远不够。实际上，要想改变行为，你还需要重新设计自己的环境。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Is there any other examples of big surprises or unintuitive results from work you've done?
turns.zh: 你们在工作中有没有遇到过其他令人大吃一惊或出乎意料的结果呢？

turns.speaker: Kristen Berman
turns.en: One big one is actually... And I'm sure people listening have worked on signup flows before. This is kind of a common question and challenge in product world. And the common thinking is, and most often correct, that if you reduce friction to the signup flow, your conversion will increase. This is kind of the law that we all live by. And yet, there is one example, one time, where this is just not true, that you can actually increase friction and increase conversion. So, actually Lenny, have I ever told you about my mother?
turns.zh: 其中一个重要问题实际上是……我相信在座听众之前都曾参与过注册流程的优化工作。这在产品设计领域是一个常见的难题和挑战。普遍观点——而且通常是正确的——认为如果能减少注册流程的阻碍，转化率就会提升。这几乎是我们都遵循的铁律。然而，确实存在这样一个例子，一个特定的案例，恰恰证明了这个观点是错误的——你完全可以增加注册流程的阻碍，同时提升转化率。那么，伦尼，我有没有跟你讲过我母亲的故事呢？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Nope.
turns.zh: 不了啦。

turns.speaker: Kristen Berman
turns.en: Okay. So, now you're thinking about my mother.
turns.zh: 好的。那么，现在你正在想我母亲的事了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh.
turns.zh: 哦。

turns.speaker: Kristen Berman
turns.en: Before, you were not thinking about... There's nothing about my mother, but I just made you think about my mother by asking you a question.
turns.zh: 之前，你并没有想起……这里并没有提到我母亲，但我只是通过问你一个问题，让你不由自主地想起了她。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Son of a gun.
turns.zh: 真是倒霉透顶！

turns.speaker: Kristen Berman
turns.en: So, when you ask a question, you can insert an idea into someone's head, you can get them thinking about something different. And so, in a sign up flow, what would you want people to be thinking about? You probably want them to be thinking about the benefits that you offer. So, if you ask them a question they can think about the benefits, it's going to increase their motivation to get over the hump of the future friction you're going to put in front of them because now they understand the benefits. So, as an example, if you go to Apartment List, they ask you questions during the signup flow that's like: What kind of apartment do you want? Do you want a studio, or a one-bedroom, a five bedroom? Do you want a patio, a basement, a view? Now, all of a sudden, I'm thinking, I'm engaging with the benefit. I understand how much supply that they have. So, if you Stitch Fix, or... Actually, Trunk Club has come out and said they did this and it increased conversion by 133%.
turns.zh: 因此，当你提出一个问题时，就能将某个想法植入用户的脑海中，促使他们转换思路。在注册流程中，你希望用户专注于什么？很显然，你希望他们关注你提供的价值主张。若通过提问让用户意识到这些好处，他们便更有动力克服未来可能遇到的阻碍——毕竟他们已清楚了解自身能获得的益处。以Apartment List为例，其注册流程会询问用户：你想要哪种户型？是单间公寓、一居室、五居室？你希望有露台、地下室还是观景窗？这些问题瞬间激发了用户的兴趣，让他们深切感受到平台的资源优势。比如Stitch Fix就曾采用这种策略，甚至Trunk Club也公开表示，通过此举转化率提升了133%。

turns.speaker: Kristen Berman
turns.en: So, asking these questions can really drive conversion. We actually did something where we put a quiz on a partner's website. It's TytoCare which is basically a device that lets you remotely connect to a physician. It's a little bit hard to use, but we wanted to help people understand the device, and we asked them questions about their medical behavior, their frequency use of technology. And for people who completed a quiz, 53% of them went on to purchase versus 37% who didn't complete. So, these type of questions can have a real impact.
turns.zh: 因此，提出这些问题确实能有效提升转化率。我们曾在合作伙伴的网站上推出过一个测试活动。TytoCare是一款能让用户远程连接医生的设备，但这款设备的使用略显复杂。我们希望帮助用户更好地了解这款设备，并向他们询问了医疗行为及科技产品使用频率等问题。完成测试的用户中，53%最终购买了该设备，而未完成测试的用户比例仅为37%。可见，类似这类问题的互动能产生切实的影响。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And so, very tactically, the idea here is you add a step to your flow that asks the user some question that isn't actually something you need an answer to, but may get them to be more excited by finishing. Is that right?
turns.zh: 因此，从策略角度来看，这里提出的思路是，在用户流程中增加一个步骤，向用户提出一些其实不需要答案的问题，但这样做可能会让他们更有动力去完成整个流程。是这样理解的吗？

turns.speaker: Kristen Berman
turns.en: Exactly, yeah. And I would say probably most teams can do this. You can replace the carousel. The carousel is something where it tells you the benefit, but we want people to actively engage with the benefit so that they're thinking about how you can improve and affect their lives.
turns.zh: 没错，确实如此。我觉得大多数团队都能做到这一点。你可以替换掉那个轮播图。轮播图的作用是向用户展示产品的好处，但我们希望用户能主动去探索这些好处，这样他们就能思考如何通过产品来提升生活质量、改变自身处境。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So, you said it's worked a couple times. It probably isn't something that usually works. Is there experience like sometimes it may work, maybe worth trying, but usually probably won't work. Is that generally right?
turns.zh: 嗯，你说这办法用过几次。可能它不是那种经常管用的方法。是不是有种经验，觉得有时候可能会有用，或许值得一试，但通常来说不太管用？这样说对吗？

turns.speaker: Kristen Berman
turns.en: We want to remove the field that was like an open text fields where we're asking people an open-ended question and we improved conversion by 40% page over page. So, for sure, some questions are harder and you should not ask them. When questions are easier and it's a drop down multiple choice, this is when you should be trying it. But definitely, the recommendation is not to ask a hard question where people have to think about it.
turns.zh: 我们想移除那种开放式文本字段，也就是那种让用户回答开放性问题的字段。通过这种改进，我们的转化率每页提升了40%。所以，确实有些问题确实比较难，应该避免提问。相反，当问题更简单，采用下拉式多选题时，就可以尝试使用这种形式。但最重要的是，建议不要设计那种需要用户深入思考的难题。

turns.speaker: Kristen Berman
turns.en: By the way, for the question that we did, that was open text, the folks on the team thought that it was an easy question. But most questions when you're asking people with an open text field, it's just not an easy question.
turns.zh: 顺便说一下，我们之前做的那个开放式文本题，团队里的人都觉得挺简单的。但大多数开放式文本题，问用户自由回答时，其实都不是容易回答的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Right. I hate those open text fields. And then, just one last, because I imagine people listening to this are like, "Oh, maybe I should run this experiment." Is the general best practice to ask a question that gets you to think about something that motivates you by finishing? What's like the rough mental model there?
turns.zh: 好的。我讨厌那些开放式文本输入框。最后再问一个问题，因为我觉得听众可能会想：“哦，也许我该做这个实验。” 一般来说，最佳做法是设计一个问题，让参与者通过完成任务来反思那些能激发他们动力的因素。那么，这个过程的大致心理模型是怎样的呢？

turns.speaker: Kristen Berman
turns.en: I think each product, obviously, will be different. One example would be, if I'm a bill pay app, you could tell me that I could pay my bill once a week, every day, every month, I could time it, but a better approach would be to ask me, "Do you want us to pay your bills immediately, or every week, or every month?" And so, what you're doing there is engaging people in the setup and actually implicitly telling them, "We can pay your bills immediately." So, would think about combining those two is showing people the benefit, like, how fast you want us to pay your bills, which gets you to think about how fast they are, and the settings which is actually you're really doing something to help the app work.
turns.zh: 我认为每款产品显然都会有所不同。举个例子，如果我是一款账单支付应用，你可以告诉我可以每周、每天、每月支付一次账单，我也可以自行设定时间，但更好的做法应该是问我：“你希望我们立即为你支付账单，还是每周、每月支付？”这样做实际上是在让用户参与到应用的设置过程中，同时暗示他们：“我们可以立即为你支付账单。” 所以，我认为将这两者结合起来的关键在于向用户展示其好处，比如你希望我们多快为你支付账单，这能让用户意识到应用的支付速度有多快，而设置选项则是在真正帮助应用正常运行。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. Before we dive even deeper into more examples, I wanted to zoom out for a moment and I'm curious just how did you even get into behavioral economics? You said you worked with Dan Ariely. How did all this come about?
turns.zh: 太棒了。在我们深入探讨更多案例之前，我想先退后一步，顺便问一下，你是如何接触到行为经济学领域的呢？你之前提到曾与丹·阿里利合作过，这一切是如何促成的呢？

turns.speaker: Kristen Berman
turns.en: Yeah, great question. So, I met Dan around 2008 and if you don't know Dan Ariely, definitely worth a Google. And at that time, he had just written his first book, Predictably Irrational, and I was a product manager at Intuit working on QuickBooks online. So, first use, customer discovery, and really after reading the book, hearing the talk, it's just like this light bulb went off and it was like... I'm talking to five to 10 customers to inform a feature, a product, and trying to come up with some insight on human behavior. And yet, there's this whole field that studied this, that has papers in thinking and studies why we behave the way we do. And so, this was like, "Wow. I can't believe we're just missing out on it in the product community." And so, I started working with Dan. We started and now, 14 years later, it's what I do; bring behavioral insights to product teams.
turns.zh: 是啊，这个问题问得太棒了。我大约在2008年认识了丹·阿里利，如果你不了解他的话，不妨去谷歌一下他。当时他刚写完第一本书《可预测的非理性》，而我还在Intuit公司担任产品经理，负责QuickBooks在线版项目。最初的使用场景是客户发现阶段。读完那本书、听过他的演讲后，我突然灵光一现——我当时正在通过访谈5到10位客户来完善某个功能或产品设计，试图洞察人类行为模式。然而，整个产品界对此却知之甚少，甚至没有相关研究成果。当时我就感叹：“天哪，产品社区怎么会错过这些宝贵的洞察呢？” 于是我开始与丹合作。14年后的今天，这份热情依然驱动着我——将行为科学的洞察注入产品团队的工作中。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And you said you were running an embedded team within Google to work on this sort of thing?
turns.zh: 还有，你说你当时在谷歌内部组建了一个嵌入式团队，专门负责这类项目？

turns.speaker: Kristen Berman
turns.en: Yeah. So, basically, Google... It was kind of our first mover in thinking about how important understanding behavioral science was to product and marketing development. And so, it was Dan and I in the beginning, and over the course of the three years we hired internal Googlers, we brought in more people on our team, and really were an internal consultant where we'd be pitched to other teams, work with them from start to end on a project. And now, Google has one of the bigger behavioral science teams that's out there.
turns.zh: 是的。所以，基本上，谷歌……它可以说是我们最先意识到理解行为科学对产品和营销开发至关重要的一家公司。最初只有丹和我两人，经过三年的发展，我们招募了谷歌内部的成员，将更多人纳入团队。当时我们实际上充当了内部顾问角色——其他团队会向我们提出需求，我们会全程参与项目的策划与执行。如今，谷歌已拥有业内规模较大的行为科学团队之一。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow. Okay. So, you've worked with how many companies at this point, roughly?
turns.zh: 哇哦。好的。那到目前为止，你大概和多少家公司合作过呢？

turns.speaker: Kristen Berman
turns.en: I'd say hundreds.
turns.zh: 我觉得有好几百个吧。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Hundreds, okay.
turns.zh: 几百个？好吧。

turns.speaker: Kristen Berman
turns.en: I mean... Yeah, hundreds.
turns.zh: 我的意思是……嗯，几百个吧。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. So, there's hundreds of companies. There's also, I imagine, hundreds of these kind of biases and heuristics and kind of behavioral expectations of people. I'm curious, out of the work that you've done, what are the most common biases, heuristics of people that you find most useful in improving product experiences in product design? What's kind of the handful that ends up being most useful?
turns.zh: 好的。所以，市面上有数百家公司。我想，人们也存在着数百种偏见、启发式思维模式以及行为预期。我很好奇，在你所做的研究中，哪些最常见的人类偏见和启发式思维模式，对产品设计中提升用户体验最为有效？最终证明最有用的那些具体是哪些呢？

turns.speaker: Kristen Berman
turns.en: Totally. And there are so many mistakes that humans make and we can call them biases, heuristics. Our team uses psychologies. What are the psychologies that drive us? And so, to tackle this, our team basically has created a model of behavior change. We call the three Bs. And this summarizes the most important psychologies that drive user that are important to the product manager and the marketers. We've used this at Google, Microsoft, LinkedIn, so all the companies that we work with, and they now use it. And so, the three B framework, first B is actually not a psychology, but it is the most important part of behavior change, and it should be obvious if you think about behavior change, behavioral economics, it is behavior. In order to change behavior, you have to pick a behavior that you want to change. So, companies are really good at outcomes, but just not as sharp at picking the behavior.
turns.zh: 完全同意。人类会犯很多错误，我们可以将这些错误称为偏见或启发式思维。我们的团队借助心理学理论开展工作。那么，驱动我们行为的关键心理学原理是什么？为此，我们团队构建了一个行为改变模型，简称"三B模型"。该模型概括了对产品经理和营销人员至关重要的用户行为驱动心理学原理。我们曾在谷歌、微软、领英等合作伙伴公司应用这一模型，如今这些公司也纷纷采用了这一框架。首先，第一个"B"并非心理学概念，但它是行为改变最核心的要素。若你研究过行为经济学，就会发现答案显而易见——行为改变的关键在于明确目标行为。许多公司善于设定最终目标，却往往忽视选定具体行为这一关键环节。

turns.speaker: Kristen Berman
turns.en: When I say behavior, I mean action. The thing that you want someone to do. By the way, the only wrong answer here is log in. It's not about logging in, it's about what you do after you log in. And when we're consulting teams, it would be like... We need to get uncomfortably specific, we say. Just really specific in the behavior. So, example, if I'm Peloton PM and I'm working on the app, I would say something like, "Within seven days of somebody starting the app, they do two 10-minute workouts with two different instructors." Now, obviously that is wildly specific and you'd probably be very happy if they did one workout with one instructor, but the reality is if you don't define that behavior you're going to change. You can't actually define the psychologies that affect someone's decision making when doing that behavior. So, that's the first B.
turns.zh: 我所说的行为，指的是用户需要完成的具体动作。比如，你希望某人做某件事。顺便说一句，这里唯一错误的答案是"登录"。这里重点不在于登录本身，而在于登录后的具体行为。在为团队提供咨询时，我们会特别强调——我们需要做到极致的具体化，在行为描述上精准到极致。举个例子，如果我是Peloton的产品经理，负责开发应用程序，我可能会设定这样的目标："用户在启动应用后的七天内，需完成两次10分钟的锻炼课程，且教练需为不同人"。显然，这个要求极其具体，如果用户只完成一次锻炼、且教练是同一个人，你可能也会感到满意。但现实是，如果不明确界定这些行为，用户的行为会随意变动。毕竟，你无法准确预测用户在执行这些行为时，其背后的心理动机和决策机制。所以，这就是第一个"B"原则。

turns.speaker: Kristen Berman
turns.en: Second B, again, is probably pretty obvious and is very critical. It's just barriers. So, we need to reduce the barriers to doing the behavior. And there are two types of barriers we look at. One is logistical. So, this is just the stuff in our way; could be entering a credit card, could be any form field. And then, the second is cognitive. So, the cognitive barriers get in our way as well. These are things like uncertainty aversion. This is optimism bias, information aversion. These are the things that would prevent... Status quo, big one. It's just you do the same thing today that you did yesterday. Your job is-
turns.zh: 接下来是第二个B，同样，这点可能相当显而易见，而且至关重要。说白了，就是各种障碍。所以，我们需要减少行为实施的障碍。我们主要关注两类障碍：一是逻辑障碍，即阻碍我们行动的具体因素，比如输入信用卡信息、填写表单等；二是认知障碍，即潜意识里的心理障碍，比如不确定性厌恶、乐观偏差、信息回避等。这些心理因素会阻碍人们采取行动。还有一个关键因素——惯性思维，即今天重复昨天的行为。你的工作就是——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Please. Can you talk about those three? Just through out there, just briefly. I'm curious about the specific biases while we're there.
turns.zh: 请问。您能谈谈那三个吗？就随便说说，简单说一下。我很好奇我们在那儿的时候会遇到哪些具体的偏见。

turns.speaker: Kristen Berman
turns.en: Yeah. So, uncertainty aversion, when something is uncertain or we're not... I'll give you an example of your Lyft. There's logistical friction which is wait time. But then, there's also this uncertainty of is it going to come on time? When is it going to come? And with this uncertainty, you're probably going to look for other options. You're going to open up Uber and say like, "Maybe it'll come faster." And so, when there is uncertainty in our life, we either look for other options, or we just don't make a decision at all. Right? This is, by the way, very big in healthcare where when you're very uncertain about something, you may not even go to the doctor, or you may just make the wrong decision.
turns.zh: 是的。所以，不确定性厌恶，当某件事存在不确定性，或者我们无法……我举个Lyft的例子。首先是后勤方面的摩擦——等待时间。但除此之外，还有不确定性，比如车会不会准时到达？什么时候到达？面对这种不确定性，你很可能会去寻找其他选择。你可能会打开Uber应用，心想：“或许它会来得更快。” 所以，当生活中的不确定性出现时，我们要么寻找其他选择，要么干脆不做决定。对吧？顺便说一下，这在医疗保健领域尤为重要。当你对某件事存在极大不确定性时，你可能根本不去看医生，或者做出错误的决定。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Got it.
turns.zh: 明白了。

turns.speaker: Kristen Berman
turns.en: And same with status quo effect where... Underlying status quo effect is this idea that we always take the path... Not always, but majority. You don't really say always when you're talking about human behavior. Human behavior is very complex. More often than not, we take the path of least resistant, that we do the thing that's easiest, and typically, the thing that's easiest is the thing that we've done yesterday and the day before. And so, when you're asking someone to do something different, which is what most product, especially startups, are trying to do, you actually have to increase their motivation or make it easier, reduce the barriers to get them to do that. And so, status quo effect is a big, big one that folks are fighting.
turns.zh: 关于现状效应也是如此……现状效应的核心在于，我们总是倾向于选择既定路径……当然并非所有人都如此，但大多数人都会如此。谈及人类行为时，很难用"总是"来概括——毕竟人类行为极其复杂。通常情况下，我们会选择阻力最小的路径，选择最简单的事物。而最简单的事物往往就是我们昨天或前天做过的。因此，当你要求人们做出改变（而这正是大多数产品团队，尤其是初创公司试图达成的目标）时，你必须增强他们的动力，或者降低障碍，让他们更容易接受新事物。现状效应无疑是人们需要克服的一大挑战。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. Thanks for sharing those. Let's keep going.
turns.zh: 太棒了。谢谢你分享这些。咱们继续吧。

turns.speaker: Kristen Berman
turns.en: Cool. So, the third B is benefits. This is where you want to increase the... Not just benefits, but the immediate benefits of doing something. We are all present bias, which means we prioritize our present self over our future self, so there are plenty of reasons that somebody, your customer, your user should take an action, but you actually have to give them a reason to take an action today.
turns.zh: 好的。那么，第三个B是好处。这里你需要强调……不只是好处，而是立即行动就能获得的好处。我们都有“现时偏好”的心理倾向，也就是说我们更看重当下的自己而非未来的自己。因此，即便客户或用户有很多理由应该采取行动，但你必须给他们一个今天就行动的充分理由。

turns.speaker: Kristen Berman
turns.en: So, as an example, if you're Asana, and if you're trying to get someone to log a task, the right thing for them to do is log the task because it's going to get their project done on time. You're going to have a collaborative and communicative team that you're going to want to be on. But one of the real reasons we may log a task is because of completion bias. We want to see the checkbox. We may log it because of social desirability bias where other people see that we're getting our work done. There's a notification that goes to my teammate when I complete something. So, these are the immediate benefits that we have to build into products and features to drive use.
turns.zh: 举个例子，如果你是Asana的用户，当你试图让别人记录任务时，正确的做法应该是让他们去记录任务，因为这有助于项目按时完成。你会希望自己的团队既善于协作又善于沟通。而我们记录任务的真正原因之一，是出于完成偏见。我们想看到那个勾选框。我们可能因为社会认同偏见而记录任务——当其他人看到我们完成了工作时，会觉得我们很能干。当我完成某项任务时，系统会向我的队友发送通知。这些都是我们必须在产品和功能中内置的即时好处，以推动用户使用。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. I definitely have completion bias. I love checking those freaking checkboxes. I know Asana is famous for that little unicorn confetti thing, right? For making you feel really good when you complete something.
turns.zh: 太棒了。我确实有完成任务的强迫症。我超爱勾选那些该死的复选框。我知道Asana因为那个小独角兽庆祝动画而出名，对吧？每次完成任务时，那种满足感简直爆棚。

turns.speaker: Kristen Berman
turns.en: Yeah. I don't know how much emphasis to put on these kind of confetti stuff. I think the idea of being done is... That psychological understanding that you completed it, confetti or not, is very powerful.
turns.zh: 是啊。我不知道该怎么看待这些庆祝用的彩纸屑之类的东西。我觉得那种"大功告成"的成就感……即便没有抛洒彩纸，也能通过心理暗示获得那种完成任务后的满足感，这真的很强大。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love confetti. Okay, so just to recap, there's the three Bs. Behavior, what is the behavior you're trying to change? And the way you described it sounds like the activation milestone. That's the way most companies think about that. Is that right?
turns.zh: 我喜欢彩纸屑。好的，让我来总结一下。就是三个B：行为，你想改变的行为是什么？从你描述的情况来看，这听起来像是激活里程碑。这也是大多数公司对此的理解，对吧？

turns.speaker: Kristen Berman
turns.en: Yeah. I would say the activation milestone and the novel thing here is just getting really specific about this behavior, so much that if you're not arguing with your teammates, you're doing it wrong.
turns.zh: 是啊。我觉得这次活动的亮点和创新之处在于，它把这种行为规范得极其细致，以至于如果你不和队友争执，那你就是做错了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: About which behavior and...
turns.zh: 关于哪种行为以及……

turns.speaker: Kristen Berman
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是啊。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: ... I imagine this often comes... Similarly to the activation kind of moment, it comes back... Working backwards from what is most likely to keep this person around long-term, kind of to keep them retained, right?
turns.zh: ……我觉得这种情况经常会出现……就像那种激活用户的关键时刻一样，它会再次浮现……我们可以从最有可能让这个用户长期留存的因素入手，也就是说要想办法留住他们，对吧？

turns.speaker: Kristen Berman
turns.en: Yeah, exactly. So, what correlates with retention and what provides an immediate value to them by doing this behavior.
turns.zh: 是啊，没错。那么，哪些因素与用户留存率相关，又有哪些行为能为用户带来即时价值呢？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. Okay. So, behavior, then barriers. How do you break down barriers, logistical and cognitive. And then, benefits. The point about being an immediate benefit is a really interesting one because, yeah, you may be like, "In a year from now I might earn some money, but I'm not going to do anything hard right now if I'm not going to make any money right now."
turns.zh: 太棒了。好的，那接下来是行为，然后是障碍。如何突破后勤和认知方面的障碍呢？然后是好处。要知道，立即获得好处这一点非常有意思。是啊，你可能会想：“一年后我或许能赚些钱，但如果现在做不了什么困难的事，就没法马上赚到钱啊。”

turns.speaker: Kristen Berman
turns.en: Exactly. And so, this is a tough one because we want to believe that people really do and use our products for the end benefit, but we really need to give people the reason to do it today.
turns.zh: 确实如此。所以这确实是个难题——我们希望人们能真正使用我们的产品，最终从中获益，但我们现在真正需要做的，是为人们提供一个即刻行动的理由。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. I want to dive into a of couple case studies of companies that I know you've worked with. Maybe before that, I thought it'd be good to ask this question about the dark side of this stuff. I imagine people often worry about, "Hey, are you just tricking people into doing things they don't want to do? That's not good." How do you think about that line?
turns.zh: 太棒了。我想深入探讨几个你曾合作过的公司的案例研究。或许在此之前，先来探讨一下这类技术的阴暗面会比较合适。我猜人们常担心："嘿，你们是不是在骗人们做他们不想做的事？这可不太好啊。" 你对这种担忧怎么看？

turns.speaker: Kristen Berman
turns.en: Yeah, it's a great question. I think, the answer to this really, with many things in life, comes down to incentives. So, what are the incentives of the product teams, of you, your manager, the team, working on this? I like to say we are what we measure, and it really matters what you measure. I'll give you a personal example.
turns.zh: 是啊，这确实是个很棒的问题。我认为，这个问题的答案——就像生活中的许多事情一样——归根结底在于激励机制。那么，产品团队、你自己、你的经理以及整个团队，致力于这项工作的动机是什么？我常说"我们就是我们所衡量的东西"，而你衡量的东西至关重要。我可以举个个人的例子说明这一点。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是啊。

turns.speaker: Kristen Berman
turns.en: LendingClub, a while ago, hired me to increase their conversion flow for borrowers. They're a lending app and they wanted to get more borrowers in the flow. The novel thing here was that they would pay me a lot of money if I hit a bump. It was like a five-point bump and zero if I didn't hit anything. [inaudible 00:25:47]
turns.zh: 不久前，LendingClub聘请我为他们的借款人提升转化率。他们是一家贷款应用平台，希望能吸引更多借款人使用平台服务。合同中的独特条款是，如果我能成功提升转化率，他们会支付我丰厚的奖金——若转化率提升5个百分点即可，若未达标则无需支付任何报酬。[此处音频中断，00:25:47处出现静音]

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That was that. That's your incentive structure.
turns.zh: 就这样吧。以上就是你的激励机制了。

turns.speaker: Kristen Berman
turns.en: Right. So, my incentive structure was to increase the conversion flow, and over the course of working with them, I became a predatory lender. I was suggesting things that the legal team was like, "No, Kristen, of course you cannot do that." Setting some contacts, I was at that time leading a Duke University lab called Common Sense Lab. It was focused on low to moderate income Americans thinking about their financial health, building savings apps for them. So, here I am, this kind of do good, non-profit, very focused on financial health of Americans, and my other hat was predatory lender for LendingClub. And so, it's really about the incentives that we're giving ourselves and our team that will drive how anything is used. Much less behavioral economics of these tactics, but generally, the success of your team.
turns.zh: 好的。所以，我的激励机制是提高转化率。在与他们合作的过程中，我逐渐变成了一个掠夺性贷款人。当时我提出的某些建议，法律团队都会说："不行，克里斯汀，你当然不能这么做。"我当时还负责管理杜克大学的一个实验室，叫做"常识实验室"。实验室专注于帮助中低收入美国人提升财务健康水平，为他们开发储蓄应用。于是，我一方面以非营利组织的身份致力于提升美国人的财务素养，另一方面又在LendingClub担任掠夺性贷款人。可见，激励机制对资源的有效利用至关重要。这里涉及的不仅是行为经济学策略，更关键的是团队的成功动力。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You may not have a clear answer to this, but any advice for setting those incentives correctly? Anything you've seen work well?
turns.zh: 您可能对此没有明确的答案，但对于如何正确设置这些激励措施，您有什么建议吗？您见过哪些实施效果良好的案例吗？

turns.speaker: Kristen Berman
turns.en: Yeah. I think for us there's two tips. One would be to set the incentive on the behavior because the behavior is going to align more with the customer outcomes than the active use or the retention. And of course... And I'm not suggesting we don't measure active use and retention in these things, you should definitely measure them, but setting the incentive, and the KPI, and the product, and the marketing team on the behavior is going to result in a more customer-friendly product and outcome.
turns.zh: 是的。我认为对我们来说，主要有两个建议。第一是将激励措施建立在用户行为之上，因为用户行为更能与客户成果产生共鸣，而非单纯关注活跃度或留存率。当然……我并不是说我们不该衡量活跃度和留存率——这些数据确实很重要，但将激励机制、关键绩效指标、产品设计以及营销团队都围绕用户行为来展开，最终会打造出更贴近客户需求的产品和服务体系。

turns.speaker: Kristen Berman
turns.en: And then, second would be increasing the duration of the incentive. So, if you're trying to hit a quarterly outcome, you're likely going to do things that will impact the short term to give that a bump. If you're trying to hit an annual or even longer outcome, you're going to be looking out for the best interest of the company and the consumers in a little bit different way.
turns.zh: 接下来，第二点是延长激励措施的持续时间。假设你正努力达成季度业绩目标，可能会采取一些短期措施来推动业绩提升。但如果你要实现年度甚至更长期的目标，就需要从更长远的角度出发，兼顾公司利益和消费者需求，采取更为审慎的策略。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. For the LendingClub example, what did you end up doing in the end, by the way? Did she just like, "Nah, let's not do this."
turns.zh: 太棒了。说到LendingClub这个例子，最后你到底怎么处理的？她是直接说"算了，还是别做这个了"吗？

turns.speaker: Kristen Berman
turns.en: I can't actually reveal the intervention that we did, but I did miss it. So, there was a five... Wait, by the way, point, not percentage bump, which is a lot, and we got 4.5. So, we almost hit it, but it's a clip, it doesn't work that way.
turns.zh: 实际上我不能透露我们采取的干预措施，但我确实错过了一个关键点。当时目标是实现5%的增长……等等，对了，是增长点数，不是百分比，不过增幅也很大，最终我们达到了4.5%。虽然差点就达成目标了，但这是个片段化的数据，实际效果可能有所偏差。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Almost sold your soul for that bump, and you didn't get there.
turns.zh: 就为了那点蝇头小利，你差点出卖了自己的灵魂，结果却功亏一篑。

turns.speaker: Kristen Berman
turns.en: I know.
turns.zh: 我知道。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It seems like [inaudible 00:28:03]
turns.zh: It seems like [inaudible 00:28:03]

turns.speaker: Kristen Berman
turns.en: It was a good lesson in incentive [inaudible 00:28:05]. And by the way, at that point, LendingClub was offering good rates to borrowers. There was efficacy in the idea of it, which is LendingClub lending to people who have lower FIGO and with better rate. And yet, you still want to have... You don't want to become the predatory lender in that situation.
turns.zh: 这是一堂关于激励机制的深刻一课[00:28:05，语音不清]。顺便说一句，当时LendingClub确实为借款人提供了优惠利率。这种模式在理念上是有效的，即LendingClub向信用评分较低的人群提供更低的贷款利率。但即便如此，你仍需谨慎行事——在这种情况下，你绝不想沦为高利贷机构。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, awesome.
turns.zh: 好的，太棒了。
