turns.zh: 如果你正在积极或被动地寻找新的机遇，不妨加入我们的求职平台。它完全免费，你可以匿名注册，甚至可以选择对特定公司隐身。随时可退出平台，只会收到你感兴趣的公司的招聘信息。欢迎访问lennysjobs.com/talent了解详情。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So, there's two companies that you worked with that I use, and I'm curious what you did for them and how you worked with them. One is TikTok, and then the other's One Medical. It'd be cool to just hear what you did for them, what they wanted your help with, and then just kind of what you took away, how it went, all that.
turns.zh: 嗯，你之前合作过的两家公司我也用过，我很好奇你为他们做了些什么，又是如何与他们合作的。一家是TikTok，另一家是One Medical。能听听你为他们做了哪些工作，客户希望你提供哪些帮助，再聊聊你的收获、合作过程以及整体体验就太棒了。

turns.speaker: Kristen Berman
turns.en: Great, yeah. So, TikTok is obviously a big platform, and with any big social media platform, they have misinformation on it. This is not just a problem with TikTok. Facebook and Twitter have it, and misinformation is growing. And so, they asked us to help decrease the spread of misinformation on their platform.
turns.zh: 太好了，我明白了。显然，TikTok是一个大型平台，任何大型社交媒体平台都存在信息误导的问题。这不只是TikTok独有的问题。Facebook和Twitter也存在类似问题，且虚假信息传播现象日益严重。因此，他们邀请我们协助减少虚假信息在其平台上的传播。

turns.speaker: Kristen Berman
turns.en: There's lots of ways that we could take that, and the first thing that we did, as we kind of do with any company, is think about what is the behavior that you want to change. And so, we narrowed on decreasing shares. So, we could have said likes. We could have said comments, or general engagement which is a broad thing, but we narrowed on decreasing the shares. So, when you're actually going to see a misinformation video, we want to decrease the number of people that share it.
turns.zh: 关于这个问题，我们可以从多个角度来分析。首先，就像对待任何公司一样，我们首先要明确希望改变的具体行为。因此，我们把重点放在减少视频的分享次数上。当然，我们也可以考虑点赞数、评论量或者整体互动量等指标，但最终我们选择专注于降低视频的分享量。这样一来，当用户看到虚假信息视频时，我们就能有效减少其传播范围。

turns.speaker: Kristen Berman
turns.en: So, that was the first step. The second step is, this three B model, how do we think about the barriers? With TikTok, the thing that you want to do is get people to do something less. When you want to get somebody to do something more, you make it easier. When you want someone to do something less, you make it...
turns.zh: 好的，这是第一步。第二步是关于这个“三B模型”，我们该如何看待其中的障碍呢？就TikTok而言，你要做的就是让用户少做一些事情。当你想让用户多做些什么时，就得想办法让这件事变得更容易；而当你想让用户少做些什么时，就得反其道而行之……

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Put up barriers.
turns.zh: 设置障碍物。

turns.speaker: Kristen Berman
turns.en: Put up barriers, yeah. Actually, a nice example of it's an elevator study where basically, you want people to use the stairs. And so, what the researchers did was make the elevator door close 16 seconds longer. So now, you get in the elevator, you're annoyed. It's harder to use the elevator, and people went to the stairs.
turns.zh: 设置障碍，确实是个好办法。有一个电梯研究的例子，研究者希望人们多使用楼梯。为此，他们把电梯门关闭的时间延长了16秒。结果发现，人们进入电梯后会感到不耐烦，觉得使用电梯变得麻烦，于是更多人选择走楼梯了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: 16 seconds, interesting number.
turns.zh: 16秒，有趣的数字。

turns.speaker: Kristen Berman
turns.en: 16 sec... We can't wait 16. And then, it's actually kind of long, though. You're standing there [inaudible 00:31:02].
turns.zh: 16秒……我们可等不了16秒啊。不过说真的，这时间确实有点长了。你就站在那儿，啥也不说[听不清00:31:02]。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So long. I'd use the stairs, yeah.
turns.zh: 再见了。我会走楼梯的，嗯。

turns.speaker: Kristen Berman
turns.en: Yeah. And so, that's kind of what we did for TikTok, which is, basically, you're in a very hot state. TikTok is a very fast platform, and so we just slowed people down. Two things. There was a label on the video, which is kind of classic in the misinformation world where you tell users that it's unverified information. And the second thing was, once you click the share button, we popped up something that said, "Are you sure?" And this was basically slowing people down. So, logistical friction, and actually cognitive friction because we're asking people to reconsider a prior decision and question their self. And so with that, both those things, the label on the video and the popup, reduced shares by 24%.
turns.zh: 是啊。所以，这就是我们在TikTok上采取的策略。基本上，用户当时处于一种非常激动的状态。TikTok是一个节奏极快的平台，所以我们就让用户慢下来。主要有两个措施。一是给视频加标签，这在虚假信息领域是经典做法，告知用户信息未经核实。二是一旦用户点击分享按钮，我们会弹出提示框问“你确定吗？”这些策略有效降低了分享量，效果显著——标签和弹窗提示共使分享量下降了24%。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow.
turns.zh: 哇。

turns.speaker: Kristen Berman
turns.en: And these are tactics that Facebook and Twitter are also using to slow people down. This was actually one of the first [inaudible 00:31:48] published studies that showed that this drove down misinformation.
turns.zh: 这些策略其实也是Facebook和Twitter用来减缓信息传播速度的手段。这是首批证明此类措施能有效减少虚假信息的研究之一。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Can you talk a bit about how you came to those two conclusions? I know you work really closely with the product team and there's this whole process you go through. How do you come up with these ideas? How many ideas did you test? Is there anything more you could share on that?
turns.zh: 能否谈谈你们是如何得出这两个结论的？我知道你们与产品团队密切合作，整个过程很复杂。你们是如何构思这些策略的？测试了多少种方案？能否分享更多相关信息？

turns.speaker: Kristen Berman
turns.en: Yeah. It's actually a pretty involved process. First, we did a literature review which is basically saying like, Look, we're not the first people to think about this. Let's talk to the expert and understand what has worked and what hasn't." So, with that, actually, one of the insights was that reminding people about their value of accuracy. So, most people want to be accurate. Most people actually don't want to share this information. And so, if you can remind people at the point of sharing... By the way, it doesn't work if you remind people before or after. It's at the point of sharing, that this is unverified information, studies have shown that this could decrease share. So, we took that piece. We also took the hot and cold state literature that says, "If you actually don't want to get someone to do something, how do you intervene?
turns.zh: 是的。这其实是一个相当复杂的过程。首先，我们进行了文献综述，基本上就是说，看看我们不是第一个想到这个问题的人。让我们和专家交流，了解哪些方法有效，哪些无效。基于此，关键的洞察之一是提醒用户重视准确性。大多数人希望信息准确，大多数人实际上不愿分享这些信息。所以，如果能在分享环节提醒用户……顺便说一句，如果在分享前后提醒，效果都不理想。正是在分享环节，告知用户信息未经核实，研究表明这能减少分享量。因此，我们采用了这一策略。我们还参考了关于“冷热状态”的文献，研究表明，如果你不想让某人采取某种行动，该如何进行干预？

turns.speaker: Kristen Berman
turns.en: So, we did this literature review. We came up with a hypothesis, and we had probably 30 different ways to implement this because the hypothesis is just a starting point. And then, we put it into quantitative research. So, we actually put five different version of the popup in front of over a thousand users, which... We got users from Prolific, which is a platform where you can easily test things.
turns.zh: 所以，我们进行了文献综述，提出了一个假设，可能有30种不同的实现方式，因为假设只是一个起点。然后，我们将其转化为定量研究。因此，我们向超过千名用户展示了五种不同版本的弹窗提示……这些用户来自Prolific平台，在那里可以轻松测试各种方案。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Prolific? Cool. I haven't heard that.
turns.zh: Prolific？不错啊。我还没听说过这个平台。

turns.speaker: Kristen Berman
turns.en: We didn't measure the idea, "Do people like this?" We measured a condition against another condition. So, relatively, what condition is more likely to work than the other condition, and that would increase our intuition than it would work in market. We're not saying that studies outside of the product are end-all be-all, but it's going to drive our intuition up a lot more.
turns.zh: 我们没有衡量“用户是否喜欢这个方案”，而是将一种条件与另一种条件进行对比。也就是说，哪种条件更有可能奏效，相较于市场上的实际效果，哪种更易推广。我们不是说产品之外的研究就是万能的，但它能极大提升我们的直觉判断。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: For the research that you did, I imagine that's a lot of the value that you and your team bring to a group. For folks that are just on their own maybe, is there any advice for how to find research on problems you're trying to solve?
turns.zh: 就你所做的研究而言，我想这正是你和团队为某个团队创造价值的重要部分。对于那些独自工作的人来说，有没有什么建议能帮助他们找到自己试图解决的问题的相关研究？

turns.speaker: Kristen Berman
turns.en: Yeah. I would say, basically, if you're looking at a new problem, it's very tempting to talk to [inaudible 00:33:53] users in the beginning. We would basically say, "Look, go spend a day on the internet googling to see what else has been done." Google Scholar is a great place to start. Hot tips would just be making sure you're searching the right keyword. So, if you're looking at something in healthcare, you'd want to know what are the buzz words for chronic care and things that would actually drive you to a meta-analysis that would summarize what's already been done. So, Google Scholar, a great place to start. And then, coming up with the hypothesis and putting them to test. We never do a UX study where we're just showing people one thing because they could really like it or hate it, but they could really like or hate all the designs. We have no idea. So, when we're doing this, we always present multiple options, and then relatively look for which one is going to drive the behavior we're intending to change.
turns.zh: 是的。我觉得基本上，如果你正在研究一个新问题，一开始就和用户交流是很有诱惑力的。我们通常会说：“去网上搜搜看有没有相关研究。”Google Scholar是个很好的起点。关键是要确保搜索的关键词准确。比如，如果你研究的是医疗领域，就要了解慢性病护理的流行术语，这些术语可能会引导你找到总结已有研究的荟萃分析。所以，Google Scholar是个很好的入口。然后是提出假设并进行验证。我们从不做那种只给用户展示一种设计然后判断他们喜不喜欢的用户体验研究，因为他们可能喜欢或不喜欢所有设计，我们根本无法判断。所以在做这类研究时，我们总会提供多个选项，然后比较哪个设计能真正促成我们想要改变的行为。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Is there a reason you did UX-oriented test versus testing the product? Is it just because they weren't ready to build an experiment in product yet?
turns.zh: 你做用户体验导向的测试而不是产品测试，是有什么原因吗？是因为产品还没准备好做实验吗？

turns.speaker: Kristen Berman
turns.en: Yeah. We actually only got two conditions in product, which for us is we would like more and it was... We don't know if we're going to get a second bat at this. So, we said, "Well, two conditions plus the control." But what should those two conditions be? So, for us, we want to de-risk the launch as much as possible.
turns.zh: 是的。我们产品里只有两个条件，对我们来说还不够，但不知道是否还有机会优化。所以我们说，“两个条件加一个对照组。”但这两个条件应该是什么？对我们来说，就是要尽可能降低产品上线的风险。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. And is that feature in the product today?
turns.zh: 太棒了。这个功能现在在产品里吗？

turns.speaker: Kristen Berman
turns.en: It is.
turns.zh: 在的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing.
turns.zh: 太棒了。

turns.speaker: Kristen Berman
turns.en: Yes, it is in the product, and they've done more global launches as well.
turns.zh: 是的，产品里有，而且他们还在全球范围内推广了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Sweet. I am clearly not sharing misinformation because I haven't seen it yet.
turns.zh: 太好了。看来我没提供错误信息，因为我还没见过。

turns.speaker: Kristen Berman
turns.en: You may not be searching the right thing. If you search medical, COVID, politics, you may get it.
turns.zh: 你可能搜索的关键词不对。如果你搜索医疗、新冠、政治，可能搜不到。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh, boy. Here comes the decline of me. Okay. So, next case study that I thought would be fun to talk about is One Medical which I'm a happy customer of. What did you do with them?
turns.zh: 天哪。我真是老了。好吧。接下来我想聊的案例研究是One Medical，我是他们的忠实用户。你们为他们做了什么？

turns.speaker: Kristen Berman
turns.en: Yeah. Basically, One Medical asked us to increase engagement. This is a classic question. How do you increase engagement in a product or service, right?
turns.zh: 是的。基本上，One Medical让我们提高用户参与度。这是个经典问题——如何提高产品或服务的用户参与度，对吧？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Engagement, meaning just using it more often?
turns.zh: 参与度，就是让用户更频繁地使用？

turns.speaker: Kristen Berman
turns.en: Right, exactly. That's the real question, what does engagement mean? Actually, a have fun exercise that people could do with their teams is if you ask everyone on the team what engagement means separately, you can compare answers and most likely, people are saying different things. And if you guys can't agree internally on what to do or what engagement means, it's very difficult to build a product by which your users understand what to do.
turns.zh: 对，就是这个问题。参与度到底意味着什么？实际上，一个有趣的练习是让团队里的每个人分别定义参与度，然后比较答案，很可能大家会说出不同的定义。如果团队内部对如何定义参与度或参与度意味着什么都无法达成一致，那么就很难打造出用户能理解该怎么做的产品。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yup.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Kristen Berman
turns.en: Yeah. So, after lots of debate, we came up with a key behavior to target. Basically, somebody setting up a doctor's appointment right after signing up for One Medical. This is really important because more likely than not, you're going to sign up for One Medical, six months later, you're going to get a fever and get sick, and are you going to remember this app that you signed up for six months ago? Probably not.
turns.zh: 是的。所以，经过多次讨论，我们确定了一个关键的优化方向。基本上，就是让用户在注册One Medical后，立即预约医生。这点非常重要，因为很可能用户注册了六个月后，才突然发烧生病，但你还能记得六个月前注册的这个应用吗？大概率记不住。

turns.speaker: Kristen Berman
turns.en: You're going to do the same thing you did before, which is call the doctor that you've normally gone to. So, really important for One Medical upfront, during onboarding, to set the mental model of what they can be used for in going to that doctor's appointment. Then, we looked to the barriers. One of the barriers, like, who is going to be your provider, your doctor. Picking somebody is hard. Finding an appointment time is hard. We're all busy people. How are you going to fit it in? Knowing actually what One Medical can help you with, also difficult. Like, what is this company thing and what should I go to them for? And then, the benefits. What are the benefits? And the benefits for using One Medical is you get your questions answered immediately. It's very simple, but you can really get your health questions and issues addressed. And so, the simple intervention we did was, just during onboarding, we asked people a few questions about their health; mental, sleep, physical. We then recommended a provider. So, instead of having lots of choice, we decreased the choice, recommended them one provider, told them why, and then recommended appointment times. And limited the amount of appointment times. It was for tomorrow. We recommended a virtual appointment so it'd be a quick thing that you could do from your home. And then, that intervention, the onboarding intervention, increased bookings by 20% during onboarding.
turns.zh: 你还是会像以前那样，直接打电话给常去的医生。所以，对One Medical来说，最重要的是在用户注册时就建立正确的预期，让他们明白这个应用能在看医生预约上提供哪些帮助。接下来，我们分析了阻碍用户使用的障碍。比如，选择医生是个难题。另外，预约时间也难协调，毕竟大家都很忙。还有，用户可能不清楚One Medical能提供哪些服务，比如这家公司的定位是什么，什么时候该用它？然后，好处部分也很重要。核心好处就是能快速解答健康问题。为此，我们在注册流程中做了几个简单干预：首先询问用户健康状况（心理、睡眠、身体方面），然后推荐一位医生，说明推荐理由，最后推荐预约时间。预约时间仅限次日，且建议采用虚拟问诊，方便用户在家完成。这些优化措施让注册期间的预约量增加了20%。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Of appointments?
turns.zh: 预约量？

turns.speaker: Kristen Berman
turns.en: Of appointments, yeah.
turns.zh: 是预约量。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: With this-
turns.zh: 通过这些措施——

turns.speaker: Kristen Berman
turns.en: Onboarding. I don't know if I went through that when I joined One Medical.
turns.zh: 注册流程优化。我不知道自己加入One Medical时有没有经历过这个流程。

turns.speaker: Kristen Berman
turns.en: This is recent.
turns.zh: 这是最近才改进的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, cool. Yeah. By the way, One Medical's awesome. As you're talking, I'm thinking if you could think about what are the five most commonly successful changes to a flow. One right now you just shared was reducing options, which is interesting.
turns.zh: 好的，不错。顺便说一句，One Medical真的很棒。你讲的时候，我就在想，如果能总结一下流程优化中最成功的五个改进点会怎样。比如你刚刚提到的减少选项，这很有意思。

turns.speaker: Kristen Berman
turns.en: Yep.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And then, another you mentioned earlier is just reminding you of maybe what you're going to get out of it at the end. I don't know. Is there anything that comes to mind of here's a subset of things that seems to often work when you're trying to improve, say, activation or conversion of a flow?
turns.zh: 另外，你之前提到过要提醒用户最终能获得什么好处。我不知道，你能不能举个例子，说明在提升用户活跃度或转化率时，哪些子集的优化措施往往比较有效？

turns.speaker: Kristen Berman
turns.en: I would caveat all this with behavior is contextual. Why we are religious about testing is because it's hard to drag and drop from different contents. So, I'd caveat with that. And of course, there are some rules of thumb. So, one thing, really, is about showing people the benefit right away, really not under or overestimating that people understand the benefit of your app. So, how do you get them to experience it immediately? I would say that that's one.
turns.zh: 我要提醒大家，用户行为是情境化的。我们之所以强调测试的重要性，是因为不同内容很难直接复制粘贴。所以这点需要注意。当然，也有一些经验法则。比如，让用户立即感受到好处很重要，既不能高估也不能低估用户对应用价值的理解。那么如何让他们立即体验到好处呢？我觉得这是一个关键点。

turns.speaker: Kristen Berman
turns.en: And then, the other is really just the reducing... I hate to sound so simplistic, but a lot of it is about making things easier logistically and cognitively, and making the benefit much more clear, salient. We say moving it from abstract to concrete. You really want to move something from the world of people can't really imagine how it would fit in their life to how does it actually fit in their life and keeping them going.
turns.zh: 然后，另一个关键点就是简化流程……我不想说得太简单，但很多时候就是要从逻辑和认知层面简化流程，让好处更清晰、更突出。我们说要把抽象概念转化为具体场景。要让用户从“这东西怎么融入我的生活”转变为“它到底怎么融入我的生活”，并持续推动他们前进。

turns.speaker: Kristen Berman
turns.en: If it's a long signup flow and people need to drop out, how do you send them reminders to pull them back in, and then when they are back in, land them on the spot that they were at. So, Wealthfront has said one of their key insights was when people dropped out of the flow, normally they would just put people back at the beginning. That's really frustrating. If you can put people back where they landed, they're more likely to continue.
turns.zh: 如果用户在注册流程中中途退出，你要如何通过提醒让他们重新加入，然后当他们回归时，再把他们带到中断的步骤。Wealthfront曾指出，他们的一个关键洞察是，用户退出流程后，通常会被带回起点。这真的很令人沮丧。如果能让用户回到他们停止的步骤，他们更有可能继续下去。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That makes sense. Reduces barriers. I'm learning.
turns.zh: 有道理。减少障碍。我学到了。

turns.speaker: Kristen Berman
turns.en: Exactly.
turns.zh: 没错。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So, there's two really interesting things you just said that I'd love to dive into a little bit. One is showing the benefit of something right away. Is there an example of that that comes to mind where you did that and it worked out really well? What's an example of showing a benefit?
turns.zh: 你刚才提到的两个很有趣的点，我很想深入探讨一下。一个是立即展示好处的例子，你能想到一个成功案例吗？能举个展示好处的例子吗？

turns.speaker: Kristen Berman
turns.en: There's two ways to do benefits. One is the actual one that a consumer has. So, Asana and the collaborative communicator versus maybe one that's more immediate. When we're thinking about more immediate benefits, this could actually be things like social norms where you're telling people everybody else is doing something, and to them the benefit of doing this is following the herd. We all, by the way, don't like to think that we're part of the herd, but we all will succumb to this at some point in our lives.
turns.zh: 展示好处有两种方式。一种是消费者实际获得的好处，比如Asana和协作通信工具；另一种是更即时的好处。当我们考虑更即时的好处时，可能涉及社会规范，比如告诉人们其他人都在做某件事，这样用户的好处就是随大流。说实话，我们都不愿承认自己是随大流的人，但人生某个阶段我们都会屈服于这种心理。

turns.speaker: Kristen Berman
turns.en: And so, one example is where we worked with a company called Study. This was a FinTech app and we're helping people to sign up or sync their bank account. Syncing their bank account is a required step in any kind of FinTech app, and yet so difficult, big drop off point. Just by reframing the choices of getting someone to think about completing a step versus the benefit that would come to them after... So, the benefit of syncing their bank account was actually huge. You'd get to see your income. You're really actually changing someone's financial picture by doing it, and they're signing up for it. They know it. But the small immediate benefit is how you're framing each step. Each step is going to give you the immediate benefit. So, for this one, it was a completion bias thing again where people are motivated to complete something. Sometimes we'll do an error message if it's really important for the app to work. And again, you shouldn't do that all the time, but if it's really important, the benefit is actually decreasing that error message on the screen. We call this Right for Wrong, doing the right thing for the wrong reason, where the right thing may be completing the flow, but the wrong reason is seeing that error message go away. Again, I would use that with caution. People will not use and love your app if you're putting error messages all over it.
turns.zh: 举个例子，我们曾与一家叫Study的公司合作。这是一款金融科技应用，帮助用户注册或同步银行账户。同步银行账户是所有金融科技应用的必经步骤，但却极易导致用户流失。通过重新构思，让用户思考完成某个步骤的意义，而非着眼于后续的好处……同步银行账户的好处其实非常大。用户可以查看自己的收入。通过这个操作，你真正改变了他们的财务状况，所以他们愿意注册。用户清楚这一点。但即时的微小好处在于如何框定每个步骤。每个步骤都要给予即时好处。所以对于这个案例，又回到了完成偏好的问题，用户被激励去完成某个步骤。有时如果应用的正常运行非常重要，我们会用错误提示。但别总这么做，如果真的很重要，减少屏幕上的错误提示才能带来好处。我们称之为“以错换对”，做正确的事却出于错误的理由。比如正确的做法是完成整个流程，但错误的理由是让错误提示消失。再强调一次，要谨慎使用这个策略。用户不会喜欢满屏错误提示的应用。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That makes sense. I think you mentioned this. I haven't mentioned, but you wrote a guest post for my newsletter. It's one of the most read posts of the newsletter on just using...
turns.zh: 嗯，有道理。我记得你提到过这点。虽然我没提过，但你确实为我的新闻通讯写过一篇客座文章。这篇文章是通讯中阅读量最高的帖子，主要讲如何利用……

turns.speaker: Kristen Berman
turns.en: Cool.
turns.zh: 不错。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: ... a lot of the... Yeah. I don't know if I told you that.
turns.zh: ……很多……对啊。我不确定有没有跟你说过。

turns.speaker: Kristen Berman
turns.en: Yeah. That's awesome.
turns.zh: 是啊，这太棒了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And it's about using these insights to improve conversion in general. So, we'll link to that in the show notes. And I think, in that post, you mentioned this concept of Right for Wrong. It might be worth spending a little more time on this, just like what does that mean and what's an example that?
turns.zh: 而且这篇文章主要讲如何利用这些洞察来提升整体转化率。所以，我们会在节目笔记中附上链接。我记得你在那篇文章里提到了“Right for Wrong”这个概念。或许值得再多花点时间解释一下这个概念，比如它的含义和具体案例？

turns.speaker: Kristen Berman
turns.en: When we think about Right For Wrong, we're helping people again do the right thing... So, this is a behavior that they want to do, but the reason is actually probably not related. So, if you think about just vaccines and what we saw here, the reason to get a vaccine is to help my neighbor and prevent them from getting sick. And yet, what happened? We gave people donut, give people free pot or marijuana. There were lottery tickets in Ohio. So, this is the Right for Wrong idea where you're really substituting... By the way, one of the bigger voting interventions is just having pizza show up at the poll line. You're motivating people to go vote not because they want to contribute to democracy, but because there's pizza in the poll line. So, at some level, we're pretty simple human where we want an immediate benefit. Clubhouse actually was an interesting example of this at some level where you saw two levels of status in Clubhouse. There were the people who were friends with the people on stage, and then there was everyone else. So, that was a motivator to be friends with more people and start following people so that you could be in that little bucket of friends with other people.
turns.zh: 当我们思考“Right for Wrong”时，我们其实是在帮助人们做正确的事……所以，这是他们想做的事，但背后的动机可能并非相关。比如我们拿疫苗接种来举例，接种疫苗的理由是帮助邻居，防止他们生病。但结果呢？我们给人们捐甜甜圈、免费大麻券，俄亥俄州还有彩票奖励。这就是“Right for Wrong”的理念，即用其他东西替代真正的原因。顺便说一句，投票干预的一个重要例子就是在投票点提供披萨。这能激励人们去投票，不是因为他们想为民主做贡献，而是因为投票点有披萨。所以在某种程度上，我们人类很简单，总是希望获得即时的利益。Clubhouse就是一个有趣的例子，它在不同层级设置了身份标识。台上的嘉宾有朋友，而其他人则没有。这就促使人们多交朋友、关注他人，以便能加入那个小圈子。

turns.speaker: Kristen Berman
turns.en: So, we're giving people kind of some other reasons to do a thing that they may want to do, but they don't necessarily have the motivation to do it right away. If you think about Peloton, yes, I want to work out. Yes, I want to have a healthy person, but maybe I want to go to the class because the instructor making a shout out, or there's some streak that I'm trying to continue. So, their right for wrong here is the real reason to work out is to improve my physical health, but while I just want that instructor to give me a shout out.
turns.zh: 所以，我们给人们一些其他理由，让他们去做想做的事，但他们未必有立即行动的动力。拿Peloton来说，用户可能想锻炼，但动机不一定强烈。也许他们想去上课，因为教练会点名，或者想保持连胜记录。所以他们的“Right for Wrong”在这里就是：真正的锻炼动机是提升身体素质，但他们更想得到教练的点名。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So, the key there, just to kind of come back to the dark side of some of this stuff, is you want to make sure the end mean is good and right, whatever it is.
turns.zh: 所以关键在于，确保最终目的是善意且正确的，无论是什么目的。

turns.speaker: Kristen Berman
turns.en: Exactly, yeah. And so, again, all these things... The possibility of using anything for negative outcomes exist, and really it's about the incentives. It's what is your incentive to drive the customer benefit, and that's really where we say you have to be measuring the customer outcomes. You have to be focused on the customer outcomes.
turns.zh: 没错，确实如此。所以，所有这些东西……利用任何手段达到负面结果的可能性都是存在的，关键在于激励机制。你的激励是什么，推动客户利益？这就是我们说你必须衡量客户成果，必须关注客户成果的原因。

turns.speaker: Kristen Berman
turns.en: Some of the toughest teams we have understanding this are non-profits. We worked with one company a while ago. We tried to get them to add a deadline because they were trying to help people sign up for interviews. So, they were basically filtering people before Staples would get them for an interview. They'd do the interview prep. They'd help them show up for the interview. But the reality is that sometimes people miss this stuff. It takes a long time to get to the interview. And so, our push to them was to add a deadline to help people show up. Sometimes we say deadlines are a gift. You're just helping people kind of prioritize this. And they said, "No. Absolutely not. We cannot add a deadline. This is just too hurtful." And the reality is when you add deadlines, and we've done this in multiple companies, where you add a deadline, more people do the thing, right? Because you're helping kind of create the right for wrong reason, giving people the wrong reason to do the behavior that they actually want to do. We added a deadline to Kiva's flow for when their borrowers were signing up and we increased their conversion. So, obviously, you can use this in ways that are unintended and it really has some upside to help people.
turns.zh: 有些最难理解这一点的团队是非营利组织。我们不久前曾与一家公司合作。我们试图让他们设置一个截止日期，因为他们当时正试图帮助人们报名参加面试。所以，他们基本上是在Staples安排面试之前就筛选求职者。他们会进行面试准备，帮助求职者按时参加面试。但现实情况是，有时人们会错过这些信息。到面试环节需要很长时间。因此，我们向他们提议增加截止日期以帮助人们按时到场。我们有时会说截止日期是礼物——你只是在帮助人们优先处理这件事。但他们拒绝了：“不，绝对不行。我们不能设置截止日期。这太伤人了。” 事实上，当你设置截止日期时（我们在多家公司都这么做过），更多人会采取行动，因为你是在用错误的理由营造正确的动机，让人们误以为是为了他们真正想做的事而采取行动。我们为Kiva的借款人报名流程添加了截止日期后，转化率大幅提升。所以显然，截止日期可能会产生意想不到的效果，但它确实有助于人们行动起来。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I imagine you're building this just like toolbox of ideas that end up working often at flow. I know you said that you can't just copy and paste. Rarely is it just like, "Oh, this worked at 10 other companies, it'll probably work here." But that's kind of a cool thing that your team's probably doing just making this big list of here's 10, 20 things that we could start with these ideas and talk about them.
turns.zh: 我猜你们把这些策略整合成一个工具箱，在流程设计中经常使用。我知道你说过不能直接复制粘贴。很少有情况是"哦，这个在其他10家公司成功了，这里应该也能行"。但这正是你们团队的巧妙之处——列出10到20个可行的创意清单，进行讨论。

turns.speaker: Kristen Berman
turns.en: Yeah. Once you understand the psychology of human behavior, you really start to understand and see patterns. We started with the idea that behavioral economics shows that people act in irrational ways, but we do it in predictable ways. And so, once you start understanding this, you can really start designing for the behavior change at this kind of predictable level.
turns.zh: 是的。一旦你理解了人类行为的心理机制，就会发现并能识别出规律。我们从行为经济学出发，发现人们会以非理性的方式行事，但这种行为具有可预测性。一旦你理解了这一点，就能在可预测的层面设计行为改变策略。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: For a product team that's listening to this and they're like, "Oh, we can't work with you guys right now. We can't afford it. We don't have time, just generally, but I want to think about this stuff and maybe implement it on my team." What would you suggest to say a PM leading a team that wants to implement some of these principles?
turns.zh: 对于听了这些内容却觉得"我们现在没法合作，负担不起，时间不够"的PM团队，我建议他们怎么做？

turns.speaker: Kristen Berman
turns.en: Yeah. I would probably start from the process angle. We have the three B framework, which again, the most important step is defining the behavior. So, if you were to do a workshop with your team on what is the uncomfortably specific behavior that you want to change and you align everyone to this, it's going to be much easier for you to change that behavior because the psychology that drive that behavior will be a better conversation and more obvious.
turns.zh: 我可能会从流程角度入手。我们的三B框架中，最重要的一步是定义行为。如果你能和团队一起参加研讨会，明确你想改变的具体行为，并让所有人达成共识，那么改变这种行为就会容易得多，因为驱动这种行为的心理机制会更清晰、更易理解。

turns.speaker: Kristen Berman
turns.en: So, first in starting with the behavior, to get everyone in a room do a small workshop. The second would be the behavioral diagnosis. And this is the toolkit in behavioral science where we study not what people say they will do, but what they actually do. And so, the behavioral diagnosis, I'd say, it's like a journey map on steroids where you're really trying to map the steps that get people to the behavior change. And again, just doing this, teams have light bulbs. And this is one of the main things that we work with teams on; we help them do the behavioral diagnosis to have those light bulbs, and then we help diagnose and design the intervention.
turns.zh: 好的，首先从行为入手，让所有团队成员参加一个小型研讨会。接下来是行为诊断。这是行为科学中的工具箱，我们研究的不是人们说他们会做什么，而是他们实际做了什么。所以，我觉得行为诊断就像是深度版的用户旅程地图，真正试图描绘出让人们实现行为改变的各个步骤。通过这样做，团队成员往往能灵光一现。这是我们与团队合作的主要内容之一——我们帮助他们进行行为诊断，激发灵感，然后再设计干预措施。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Can you talk a bit more about this behavioral diagnosis step? What actually happens there?
turns.zh: 你能详细讲讲这个行为诊断步骤吗？具体怎么操作的？

turns.speaker: Kristen Berman
turns.en: There's kind of two steps. One, you can outline the full high level flow where you're saying maybe there's 50 steps in getting to the behavior, and you can do this before they hit your product, too. But when we're working with just a very kind of... We want to help a team grow their product versus develop a new product, if it's just about growing and improving the current product, we'll do a deck of 200, 300 slides of screenshots where it's just very detailed analysis of the steps that it takes to get to the behavior change. And then, we overlay the psychologies that are driving people at each step. This actually takes a really long time, but the light bulbs of how you actually get to that beha... As I said, behavior change isn't easy. It's complex. It's hard. It's noisy. And so, you have to understand the steps that get you there before you're trying to change it.
turns.zh: 大致分两步。第一步，你可以勾勒出整个高层流程，比如说实现某个行为可能需要50个步骤，这可以在产品上线前就完成。但当我们面对的是一个正在成长的团队，帮助他们改进现有产品而非开发新产品时，我们会制作200到300页的幻灯片，详细分析实现行为改变的各个步骤。然后，我们会叠加每个步骤中影响人们行为的各种心理因素。这确实需要很长时间，但通过理解实现行为改变的各个步骤，才能真正找到突破口。毕竟，行为改变并不容易——它复杂、困难、充满阻碍。在尝试改变行为之前，你必须先理解达成目标的步骤。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow, that sounds really useful. So, you go through the product, make a screenshot of every little step, and then connect what barrier's keeping them from progressing. Is that roughly right?
turns.zh: 哇，这听起来真的很有用。那你们会逐一分析产品中的每个小步骤，然后找出阻碍他们前进的障碍，对吗？

turns.speaker: Kristen Berman
turns.en: Exactly, yeah. So, maybe in a health app, it's information aversion. They don't actually want to see their test result. That's a step, and then we attach that psychology to that step and now we can have a brainstorm about, "Well, what would help decrease information aversion to get them over the next hump?"
turns.zh: 没错。比如在健康类应用中，可能是用户对信息的抗拒，他们不想看到自己的检测结果。这就是一个步骤，然后我们将这种心理因素与该步骤相结合，接着就能集思广益，思考如何减少信息抗拒，帮助用户跨越下一个障碍。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What's cool about this is you could just... As a team, you have all these things you're trying to improve, all these flows and steps and things like that, and basically, these psychologies, as you call them, are useful to just anything you're trying to optimize. I imagine there's just like a list on Wikipedia of all these human psychologies and biases. I imagine a better way to learn about this is to take your course. So, maybe it's a good time to just chat about the course that you teach versus coming in house and working with the team. Can you talk a bit about that? Or are those the same thing?
turns.zh: 这项技术的妙处在于，团队在改进产品、优化流程等方面，遇到的所有难题都可以借助这些心理因素来分析。我想维基百科上应该有完整的人类心理学与偏好列表。要深入了解这些知识，最好的办法就是参加你的课程。所以，现在或许可以聊聊你教授的课程与现场辅导的区别。能谈谈这两者的区别吗？或者它们本质上是一回事？

turns.speaker: Kristen Berman
turns.en: No, that's perfect. Yeah, so we have a... Thanks for the tee up, Lenny. Appreciate it. We have a bootcamp course, which basically is a self-paced online course that you can go in and understand. It has a lot of our case studies, many of them I didn't talk about here, and we walk you through the process. You'll have an intro call with us. There's a Slack group. There's office hours really trying to help people go through the process of behavioral design yourself, and it really brings these concepts to life and helps you apply them to your product. So, I think, starting with that bootcamp is a great place for designers, product managers, marketers, researchers to start. I can send you this. We have a Sweet 16, some of the 16 biases that we refer to most. The three Bs is an easy way to evaluate a product if you're just starting, but as you get deeper, these different psychologies will pop up.
turns.zh: 没错，太完美了。嗯，所以我们有一个……感谢你介绍，莱尼。我很感激。我们有一个训练营课程，基本上是一个自定进度的在线课程，你可以登录了解相关内容。里面有很多我们的案例研究，其中很多我在这里没有提到，还会带你逐步完成整个过程。你会和我们进行一次介绍性通话。还有一个Slack群组。每周的办公时间专门帮助大家自己探索行为设计的流程，能让这些概念生动起来，并帮助你将其应用到你的产品中。所以，我认为，从这个训练营入手，对于设计师、产品经理、市场营销人员和研究人员来说都是一个很好的起点。我可以把资料发给你。我们还有“十六大偏见”（Sweet 16），这些是我们最常提到的16种偏见。三个B原则（three Bs）是刚开始评估产品时一个简单的方法，但随着你深入了解，不同的心理学概念就会逐渐浮现。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. Please send that and we will link to it in the show notes. Just a couple more details in this course, how often do you run it? How long does it take generally for folks to take?
turns.zh: 太棒了。请把资料发送给我们，我们会在节目笔记中附上链接。关于这个课程，还有几个细节，你们的课程多久举办一次？通常人们完成课程需要多长时间？

turns.speaker: Kristen Berman
turns.en: Yeah. So, once a year we'll do a cohort course that's a little bit more in depth, but the best way is this kind of self-paced course. It's a eight-week course and we give you a month extra to go through it. There's 16 modules and there's homework throughout it that you can post in Slack and get feedback from behavioral scientists. So, a pretty interactive course, but you can go through it on your own and even share with your team. We do group things. We'll do like a team of 10, and then we can give you a private office hour where we just riff with you on your product challenges.
turns.zh: 是的。我们每年会举办一次深度课程，但最好的方式是这种自定进度的课程。这是一个为期八周的课程，我们会给你额外一个月的时间完成学习。课程包含16个模块，整个过程中还有作业，你可以在Slack上发布并获得行为科学家的反馈。所以，这是一个互动性很强的课程，但你也可以自行学习，甚至与团队分享。我们会组织10人的小组，然后为你们提供私人办公时间，与你们一起探讨产品挑战。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. And folks can find that at irrationallabs.com. Is that right?
turns.zh: 太棒了。人们可以在irrationallabs.com上找到相关信息，对吧？

turns.speaker: Kristen Berman
turns.en: Yeah. Thanks again for this.
turns.zh: 是的。再次感谢。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: irrationallabs.
turns.zh: irrationallabs。

turns.speaker: Kristen Berman
turns.en: Yeah, irrationallabs.com is the spot, and if you... Probably signing up for a newsletter is also... We publish all of our research there and other kind of fun behavioral insights.
turns.zh: 是的，irrationallabs.com就是这个入口，如果你……可能订阅时事通讯也很不错。我们在那里发布所有研究成果和其他有趣的行为洞察。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Sweet. Well, with that, we've reached our exciting lightning round.
turns.zh: 好的。那么，接下来我们要进行激动人心的闪电问答环节了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So, I'm just going to ask you a bunch of quick questions. Whatever comes to mind, fire away and we'll just go through them real fast. Sounds good?
turns.zh: 那么，我要问你一堆快速问题了。想到什么就说什么，我们会快速过一遍。听起来不错吧？

turns.speaker: Kristen Berman
turns.en: Great.
turns.zh: 好的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, cool. What are two or three books that you recommend most to other people?
turns.zh: 好的，很酷。你最推荐给别人的两三本书是什么？

turns.speaker: Kristen Berman
turns.en: I would be [inaudible 00:52:17] not to say Predictably Irrational. I think this is a great starter book for people getting interested in the field. Influence is also a great starter book for people getting interested in the field. Many times you read Influence and you change Your Career. It's a really powerful book. And then, the under-talked about one is [inaudible 00:52:35] author Robert Frank. He wrote Darwin Economy, and he talks more about kind of status, and social norms, and how this drives a lot of our behavior. So, I'd recommend Robert Frank as an author in Darwin Economy.
turns.zh: 我会推荐[听不清00:52:17]《可预测的非理性》。我认为这本书对于刚开始对这个领域感兴趣的人来说是一个很好的入门书籍。《影响力》也是一个很好的入门书籍。对于刚开始对这个领域感兴趣的人来说。很多时候你读了《影响力》之后，会改变你的职业生涯。这是一本非常有力的书。然后，不太被提及的是[听不清00:52:35]作者罗伯特·弗兰克。他写了《达尔文经济学》，更多地讨论了地位和社会规范，以及这些如何驱动我们的很多行为。所以，我推荐罗伯特·弗兰克和他的《达尔文经济学》。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What's another favorite podcast other than the one you're currently on?
turns.zh: 除了你现在参加的这个播客，还有其他你最喜欢的播客吗？

turns.speaker: Kristen Berman
turns.en: Science of Change is my actual podcast, so a little self-promotion. We interview product leads and talk about what they've done in their product. And then, the other one is, No Stupid Question. This is by the Freakonomics. Stephen Dubner and Angela Duckworth come together and just answer questions about behavior change.
turns.zh: 《变革科学》是我主持的播客节目，所以先自我宣传一下。我们会采访产品负责人，探讨他们在产品开发中的实践经验。另外还有《无需愚蠢的问题》这个节目，由《魔鬼经济学》的斯蒂芬·达布纳和安吉拉·达克沃斯共同主持，专门解答行为改变相关的问题。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What's a favorite recent movie or TV show?
turns.zh: 你最近最喜欢的电影或电视剧是什么？

turns.speaker: Kristen Berman
turns.en: I love The Rehearsal. This is-
turns.zh: 我喜欢《排练人生》。这部剧——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I can see you loving it.
turns.zh: 我能想象你会喜欢它。

turns.speaker: Kristen Berman
turns.en: Yeah. So, it's basically made me feel that it's rehearsing life. And I think, sports, it's so obvious you want to practice. I just started ping pong lessons actually, and I'm doing the same stroke for an hour. But in life, we don't rehearse as much. I don't write an email a hundred times, and then practice sending it. And so, I think there's probably an opportunity for us all to learn some lessons from that.
turns.zh: 是啊。这部剧让我感觉它在排练生活。我觉得体育运动中，大家很清楚需要不断练习。我最近刚开始学乒乓球，连续一个小时都在重复同一个动作。但在生活中，我们却很少这样刻意练习。我不会把一封邮件写一百遍再练习发送。所以我觉得我们或许都能从中汲取一些启发。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Have you seen Nathan For You, his other show?
turns.zh: 你看过他的另一部节目《为你服务》吗？

turns.speaker: Kristen Berman
turns.en: I have, yeah. The Rehearsal was just so compelling and I'm not usually somebody who watches media, so this was mind blowing. I loved it.
turns.zh: 看过了。《排练人生》太引人入胜了，而我通常不怎么追剧，所以这部剧让我惊叹不已。我超爱它。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I actually like Nathan For You better.
turns.zh: 但我其实更喜欢《为你服务》。

turns.speaker: Kristen Berman
turns.en: Oh, interesting. Okay.
turns.zh: 哦，有意思。好的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是啊。

turns.speaker: Kristen Berman
turns.en: I'll give another...
turns.zh: 我再举个例子……

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What a weird show, but I love it. Okay, next. What is a favorite interview question that you like to ask?
turns.zh: 这部剧太奇怪了，但我超爱它。好的，下一个问题。你最喜欢问的面试问题是什么？

turns.speaker: Kristen Berman
turns.en: So, interview for... I'll take this as interviews for people when we're hiring. I would caveat to say, interviews, actually we know, don't predict job performance. So, very little to no evidence would say interviews will predict how I perform on the job.
turns.zh: 所以，面试……我把这理解成招聘时的面试。我得提醒一下，面试其实并不能预测工作表现。所以几乎没有证据表明面试能预测一个人在工作中的表现。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Shush. Just kidding.
turns.zh: 嘘。开玩笑的。

turns.speaker: Kristen Berman
turns.en: We use skill assessments and trials as ways to predict job performance, but interviews are good at predicting affinity and culture fit. And so, if you want to ask a question about that, one of my favorite questions is just, what is a personality trait that defines you? So, really, one that you are filled with strength, but that also can be seen as something you're working to improve. So, for me, I may be confident, but that may mean that I'm not listening. And so, we have really strong personality. People are really quick at answering this question. They really know the thing that they do good but also could hurt them, and I find that it helps understand a person a little bit easier and faster.
turns.zh: 我们用技能评估和试用来预测工作表现，但面试能有效预测求职者的亲和力和文化适应度。所以如果你想问这个问题，我最喜欢的一个问题是：“你最典型的个性特征是什么？” 就是那种你引以为傲，但同时也可能需要改进的特质。比如我可能很自信，但这也意味着我不善于倾听。这样我们就能更深入、更快速地了解一个人。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Last question, who else in the industry do you most respect as a thought leader?
turns.zh: 最后一个问题，行业内你最尊敬的思想领袖是谁？
